Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) is a well-established treatment modality for a variety of malignant diseases as well as for inborn errors of the metabolism or immune system. Regardless of disease origin, good clinical effects are dependent on proper immune reconstitution. T cells are responsible for both the beneficial graft-versus-leukemia (GVL) effect against malignant cells and protection against infections. The immune recovery of T cells relies initially on peripheral expansion of mature cells from the graft and later on the differentiation and maturation from donor-derived hematopoietic stem cells. The formation of new T cells occurs in the thymus and as a byproduct, T cell receptor excision circles (TRECs) are released upon rearrangement of the T cell receptor. Detection of TRECs by PCR is a reliable method for estimating the amount of newly formed T cells in the circulation and, indirectly, for estimating thymic function. Here, we discuss the role of TREC analysis in the prediction of clinical outcome after allogeneic HSCT. Due to the pivotal role of T cell reconstitution we propose that TREC analysis should be included as a key indicator in the post-HSCT follow-up. TREC transplantation immune reconstitution 1. Allogeneic Stem Cell Transplantation Over the past five decades, progress within the field of allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) has been astonishing, making it one of current medicine’s fastest expanding disciplines. Advances have markedly reduced risks, improved outcome, and widened the indications for the procedure. HSCT is currently a valid second or third line option for life-threatening conditions when no alternative treatments are available. The difficulty in foreseeing certain complications post-HSCT, such as relapse and infectious complications, is one of the main problems. 1.1. Indications for Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation (HSCT) Initially, HSCT was restricted to patients with acute leukemia, severe aplastic anemia (SAA), or severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) [ 1 , 2 ]. Over the years indications for treatment have widened to chronic leukemias, lymphomas, multiple myeloma, myelodysplastic syndromes, and diverse forms of inherited metabolic, hematologic and immunologic disorders. Additionally, HSCT has been evaluated—with encouraging results—as a treatment for other diseases not conventionally considered for transplant, for instance renal cell carcinoma, sickle cell anemia, beta thalassemia major, and some autoimmune disorders [ 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ]. Clinical HSCT is a quickly changing field with new methods, guidelines and treatment modalities frequently presented into routine practice. The European group for Blood and Marrow Transplantation (EBMT) and its American equivalent, Center for International Blood and Marrow Transplant Research (CIBMTR), frequently update guidelines and recommendations regarding the current practice of and indications for HSCT [ 8 , 9 ]. 1.2. Conditioning Therapy A preparative treatment (conditioning) starts the HSCT procedure. It aims to prevent graft rejection and, in malignancies, to reduce the relapse risk. Initially, total body irradiation (TBI) and high dose cyclophosphamide (Cy) were used as separate conditioning regimens and were later combined for better effect [ 10 , 11 ]. Results were promising; more than half of the initial patients remained disease-free five years after transplant [ 12 ]. Introducing the alkylating agent busulfan (Bu) in later transplants offered an alternative to the logistically more demanding TBI-based regimens [ 13 , 14 ]. As early as the 1950s it was discovered that HSCT provided an additional anti-leukemic effect to that delivered by the myeloablative conditioning alone [ 15 , 16 ]. It eventually became clear that sustained disease remission after HSCT was highly dependent on a continued reaction between the allogeneic immune system and the malignant recipient cells [ 17 , 18 , 19 ]. Based on these findings, new conditioning regimens were developed [ 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 ]. These new non-myeloablative or reduced-intensity conditioning (RIC) regimens were associated with a significant reduction of transplant-related mortality (TRM). This development also made HSCT available for new cohorts of patients for whom the treatment had previously not been considered a safe option, i.e. older patients or those with co-morbidity. Conditioning regimens are, in some instances, combined with the use of inhibiting monoclonal or polyclonal antibodies against T cells [ 24 ]. The main effect of the anti-T cell serotherapy is to prevent rejection by a reducing patient T cell numbers. However, anti-T cell serotherapy may also reduce the risk for graft-versus-host-disease (GVHD) through a delayed suppressive effect on donor T cells. 1.3. Infectious Complications The first months post-HSCT are characterized by profound immunodeficiency, in which the patients are at risk of opportunistic infections. Susceptibility to microbial pathogens decreases gradually as the immune system regains its functionality. Different periods can be distinguished based on the incidence of specific infections after HSCT. The predominance of certain pathogens in each period is a reflection of the type of cell subset deficiency post-HSCT. Not only immune reconstitution is linked to the occurrence of infections post-HSCT. There is also an association between acute GVHD and an increased predisposition to infections. This is thought to be a consequence of the immune modulatory effect of the ongoing systemic inflammation. However, the disturbance of epithelial barriers during conditioning is also a contributing factor [ 25 , 26 ]. In addition, the immunosuppressive drugs used to treat GVHD impair the immune system’s ability to combat infections. 1.4. T Cells—The Double Edged Sword GVHD, i.e., an unwanted immunologic reaction of donor lymphocytes against patient tissue, remains one of the major obstacles post-HSCT, as it causes significant morbidity and mortality. GVHD is seen in both an acute and chronic form, with individual symptoms and diverse pathophysiological mechanisms, which are not all well understood [ 27 ]. Most patients undergoing HSCT receive continuous immunosuppressive treatment during the first 3–6 months post-HSCT to prevent an allogeneic response against healthy tissue. Methotrexate (MTX) and/or cyclosporine A (CsA) is mostly used. All currently available GVHD prophylaxis options inhibit T cell reactivity [ 28 , 29 , 30 ]. Donor T cells can be inactivated for a long period through administration of neutralizing anti-T cell antibodies, either ex vivo or in vivo. These approaches are collectively termed T cell depletion. While they have the potential to eliminate the risk for GVHD, there is also a significantly increased risk of relapse. In parallel with the development of more effective immunosuppressive protocols, advances in human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-typing have significantly contributed to reducing the incidence and severity of GVHD, increasing the rates of engraftment and improving overall survival (OS) [ 31 , 32 , 33 ]. The fundamental treatment option for acute GVHD is still systemic administration of corticosteroids in addition to standard immunosuppression protocols. The effectiveness of HSCT against malignant disorders is dependent on the immunological response between donor-derived lymphocytes and neoplastic cells. This is referred to as the graft-versus-leukemia (GVL) or graft-versus-tumor (GVT) reaction, and explains why HSCT, despite the risk of severe complications, still offers a survival advantage for patients with late-stage malignant disorders when compared to other treatments. Several observations have led to the general recognition of the importance of this phenomenon. In the clinical setting, it was noted that patients who developed GVHD after HSCT had a significantly lower risk of relapse than those who did not show any symptoms of GVHD [ 18 , 19 , 34 ]. Analogously, it was shown that discontinuation of immunosuppression, with the resulting occurrence of GVHD, could be used to re-establish remission in the case of relapsed leukemia after HSCT [ 35 , 36 , 37 ]. The vital role of allo-reactive T cells in GVT reaction and GVHD is illustrated by the fact that both processes are virtually absent in transplantations with grafts fully depleted of T cells [ 38 ]. In addition, they seem to depend strongly upon some degree of histo-incompatibility between donor and recipient. There is also data suggesting that NK cells may contribute to the GVT reaction. This seems to be more pronounced against malignant cells of the myeloid lineage through inhibitory and activating NK cell receptors [ 39 , 40 , 41 ]. The GVT effect is in many cases associated with ongoing GVHD, presumably because of common elements in the mechanism of action [ 18 , 19 , 38 , 42 ]. However, this seems only to be the case if the GVH reaction is initiated against host-specific antigens expressed by malignant cells as well as healthy host cells [ 43 , 44 , 45 ]. It is also reasonable to conclude that these antigens often consist of minor histocompatibility antigens (MiHA) rather than HLA, as the GVT effect is present in transplantations with HLA-identical siblings and there does not seem to be a significant difference in the relapse rate between HSCT with HLA mismatched (MM) and fully matched donors [ 46 ]. Moreover, some antigens are only expressed on tumor cells. These tumor-specific or tumor-associated antigens do not seem to be able to autonomously elicit an allogeneic reaction but may contribute to the GVL effect once an immune response against MiHA has been established [ 47 , 48 , 49 , 50 , 51 ]. Many investigators believe that the GVT effect may be separated from GVHD and this is currently the subject of active research.

extracted_data.document_summary: This review investigates the utility of T cell Receptor Excision Circles (TRECs) and other markers (TCR diversity, CD31, PTK7) for monitoring thymic output and T-cell reconstitution after allogeneic Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation (HSCT). It examines TRECs as a predictive marker for post-HSCT complications like infections, relapse, and Graft-versus-Host Disease (GVHD), and for clinical outcomes including overall survival. The study also explores clinical factors influencing TREC levels, such as recipient age, conditioning regimen, stem cell source and dose, and pre-transplant thymic activity, and discusses TREC's broader diagnostic utility in congenital immunodeficiencies, HIV infection, and autoimmune diseases, advocating for its inclusion in post-HSCT follow-up.

treatment_details.dose_specificity: This review primarily discusses various conditioning regimens employed in Allogeneic Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation (HSCT), including total body irradiation, cyclophosphamide, busulfan, non-myeloablative or reduced-intensity conditioning (RIC), and anti-T cell serotherapy, aimed at preventing graft rejection and reducing relapse risk. It notes that a higher dose of CD34+ peripheral blood stem cells (e.g., >10^7 per kg body weight) has been associated with higher TREC levels, suggesting a dose threshold. Immunosuppressive drugs like corticosteroids and cyclosporine are mentioned in the context of GVHD prevention and treatment. However, specific dose-response relationships for HSCT or its components are not consistently reported, and the findings are often contradictory across studies due to variations in protocols and lack of randomized trials. The document focuses on monitoring applications rather than detailing specific therapeutic intervention doses.

analyzed_biomarkers.measured_tissue_or_fluid: Peripheral blood, Dried blood spots, Circulation.
analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: DNA copy quantification (PCR-based methods, including real-time PCR with TaqMan probes) or Level.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Lower, higher, unchanged, varied, or absent.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Discussed as an indicator of newly formed T cells; diluted with each cellular division; concentration levels can be expressed as TREC per cell count, TREC per mL/µL of blood, or TREC per µg of DNA. Shows 100% sensitivity for SCID screening (100% specificity with IL7). Decreased in HIV-infected patients but rapidly increased after treatment. Marked reduction in 51 rheumatoid arthritis patients vs 47 healthy controls; no reduction in 70 children with juvenile idiopathic arthritis vs 110 healthy controls. Decreased significantly in multiple sclerosis patients. Significant correlation with naive T cell numbers and a broader TCR repertoire post-transplant. Normal pre-transplant TREC correlated with higher post-transplant TREC and normal T cell count. Low TREC levels correlated with severe opportunistic infections, and lower pre-transplant TREC values associated with increased incidence of severe bacterial and CMV infection. High TREC values associated with better survival. Effective TREC recovery at 6, 9, 12 months post-transplant had 3-, 4-, 9-fold lower risk of severe infections respectively. TREC recovery at 6 months predicted non-relapse mortality and overall survival (OS). Patients who relapsed had significantly lower sjTREC levels post-transplant; higher incidence of relapse associated with lower TREC levels. Strong correlation with reduced transplant related mortality (TRM). CMV clearance was higher in patients with TREC levels above 2000 copy/µg DNA. Improved OS and PFS associated with higher TREC levels. Patients remaining TREC negative for >1 year developed acute GVHD grade II and III. Negatively correlated with recipient age pre- and post-transplantation. Significantly higher in HSCT patients receiving Reduced Intensity Conditioning (RIC) in some studies, but with contradictory findings. Significantly higher in patients receiving >10^7 CD34+ peripheral blood stem cells per kg body weight (suggesting a threshold effect). Higher in bone marrow graft recipients compared to peripheral blood stem cell (PBSC) graft recipients in some studies, but with conflicting results. Strong association between acute GVHD and delayed thymic function; chronic GVHD also impacts TREC levels. Low, almost immeasurable, TREC levels significantly correlated to the occurrence of severe infections. Absent levels found in 5 out of 21 patients who relapsed due to mixed chimerism. High pre-transplant TREC levels correlated with better overall survival (OS), decreased incidence of severe acute and chronic GVHD, lower opportunistic infections, and a reduced risk of death/relapse.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Extrachromosomal DNA excision circles generated during T cell receptor (TCR) gene rearrangement in the thymus, serving as a direct marker of recent thymic emigrants (RTE); indirectly assesses thymic output and T cell maturation. Reliably estimates amount of newly formed T cells and indirectly thymic function.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Post-allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) follow-up, during immune reconstitution; screening for congenital immunodeficiency (SCID); monitoring HIV infection before and during treatment; assessing pathophysiology in autoimmune diseases (rheumatoid arthritis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, multiple sclerosis); monitoring T cell reconstitution and thymic output after HSCT, including impact of recipient age, conditioning regimen (RIC/MAC), stem cell source (BM/PBSC) and dose, occurrence of acute/chronic Graft-versus-Host Disease (GVHD), infections, prolonged mixed chimerism, relapse, and pre-transplant thymic activity.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Predictive marker for complications (e.g., relapse, infectious complications, GVHD) and overall clinical outcome (OS, PFS, TRM) after HSCT; proposed as a key indicator for post-HSCT follow-up. Best non-invasive screening tool for SCID (especially with IL7); assesses HIV effect on thymic activity; implicated in autoimmune disease pathophysiology. Predicts immune recovery, T cell recovery, and various clinical outcomes (infection, relapse, survival) after HSCT; indicates delayed thymic function with GVHD and compromised thymic output with chronic GVHD. Predicts severe infections post-HSCT; associated with faster immune reconstitution in pediatric patients with prolonged mixed chimerism. Pre-transplant levels provide clinically relevant information for transplant outcome, predicting better overall survival, reduced severe GVHD, fewer opportunistic infections, and a reduced risk of death/relapse.

analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Genetic sequencing/analysis (spectratyping or sequencing of CDR3 of the beta chain).

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Correlates directly with thymic output; broader.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Levels of diversity depend mainly on the ability of the thymus to export new naive T cells. Broader TCR repertoire observed in CD31+thymic naive CD4+ T cell subsets compared to CD31-central subsets; higher TCR diversity in long-term after HSCT in patients with higher TREC values. A rapid increase reported by some studies in HSCT patients receiving Reduced Intensity Conditioning (RIC).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: The variety of T cell receptor sequences, which determines the breadth of immune recognition and protection against diverse pathogens. Reflects the ability of the thymus to export new naive T cells (thymic output).
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Indirectly assessing thymic output and T cell receptor repertoire reconstitution after Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation (HSCT); assessment of age-related changes; evaluating HSCT with Reduced Intensity Conditioning (RIC).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Serves as an alternative method to indirectly assess thymic output, reflecting the thymus's ability to export new naive T cells, crucial for adaptive immunity and long-term immune protection; indicates effective T cell reconstitution post-HSCT.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Unreliable as a direct measure of RTE.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Cannot accurately measure recent thymic emigrants (RTE) as they can have a longer life span, may proliferate, convert into memory T cells, or memory cells may acquire naive-like phenotypes.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Immature T cells that have not yet encountered their cognate antigen; typically indicative of new T cell output from the thymus.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Evaluating thymic output and T cell recovery after Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation (HSCT).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Not a reliable indicator for evaluating thymic output due to various confounding factors affecting their count and phenotype.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: CD31+ thymic naive CD4+ T cell subsets contain higher sjTREC than CD31- central naive CD4+ T cell subsets. Frequency in peripheral blood decreases with age. Displays a broader TCR repertoire in CD31+ cells. Telomere length and telomerase activity were higher in CD31+ compared to CD31- naive T cells.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: A transmembrane glycoprotein used to subdivide CD4+ naive T cells into thymic (CD31+) and central (CD31-) subsets, indicating lower replicative history in CD31+ cells.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: As a surrogate marker for assessing RTE; age-related changes in naive T cell populations.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Suitable candidate to assess thymic output, although not all CD31+ cells are necessarily RTE; indicates lower replicative history in the CD31+ subset.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: PTK7+ naive T cells contain higher levels of TRECs. PTK7+ cells produce less IL-2 and IFN gamma compared to the PTK7- subset.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: A novel phenotypic marker that identifies recent thymic emigrants (RTE) based on differential TREC content and cytokine production.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: As a novel marker for identifying RTE.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Used in combination with TREC for SCID screening, yielding 100% specificity. Sensitivity for IL7 alone was 85%.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Cytokine involved in lymphocyte development and survival.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Pilot study for screening congenital severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Used as part of a screening tool for SCID, improving specificity when combined with TREC.

analyzed_biomarkers.measured_tissue_or_fluid: CD31+ vs CD31- naive T cells.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Higher in CD31+ compared to CD31- naive T cells.

analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Comparison of CD31+ thymic and CD31- central naive CD4+ T cell subsets.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates a lower replicative history for CD31+ thymic naive T cells.

analyzed_biomarkers.measured_tissue_or_fluid: CD31+ vs CD31- naive T cells.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Higher in CD31+ compared to CD31- naive T cells.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Maintains telomere length, indicating replicative capacity and history.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Comparison of CD31+ thymic and CD31- central naive CD4+ T cell subsets.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates a lower replicative history for CD31+ thymic naive T cells.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: PTK7+ cells produce less IL-2 compared to the PTK7- subset.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Cytokine involved in T cell proliferation and differentiation.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Distinguishing PTK7+ from PTK7- naive T cell subsets.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Aids in identifying recent thymic emigrants (RTE) via PTK7 expression.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: PTK7+ cells produce less IFN gamma compared to the PTK7- subset.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Pro-inflammatory cytokine crucial for innate and adaptive immunity.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Distinguishing PTK7+ from PTK7- naive T cell subsets.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Aids in identifying recent thymic emigrants (RTE) via PTK7 expression.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Detected earlier than TREC in patients receiving double cord blood grafts. A significant association with TREC was reported 6 months after transplantation. Efficiency of CMV clearance was higher in patients with TREC levels above 2000 copy/µg DNA.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Mediates immune response against Cytomegalovirus infection.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Recovery after double cord blood transplantation (CBT); assessment of CMV clearance.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Associated with CMV clearance efficiency and improved overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) in post-transplant patients.
